title: In re Morrill, Alfred, Dec'd, BIIA Dec., 29,704 (1970)
text:
Morrill, Alfred, Dec'd
COURSE OF EMPLOYMENT (RCW 51.08.013; RCW 51.08.180(1))
Lunch period (RCW 51.32.015; RCW 51.36.040)
Coverage during a lunch period on the employer's premises is no greater than during the
work period. A worker is not entitled to coverage if the injury results from a wholly
independent act of the worker for his own benefit, if the worker's act has no connection
with his work or meal, and if the worker's act places him in a more dangerous position
than was required of him during the meal period. ….In re Alfred Morrill, Dec'd, BIIA
Dec., 29,704 (1970) [special concurrence]
Scroll down for order.

BEFORE THE BOARD OF INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE APPEALS
STATE OF WASHINGTON
1
IN RE: ALFRED MORRILL DEC'D ) DOCKET NO. 29,704
2
)
3
CLAIM NO. F-558192 ) DECISION AND ORDER
4
5
APPEARANCES:
6
7 Widow-petitioner, Maida L. Morrill, by
8 Brodie, Fristoe & Taylor, per
9 Donald W. Taylor, and
10 Miller, Howell and Watson, per
11 Lembhard G. Howell
12
13 Employer, International Paper Company, by
14 McLean, Klingberg & Houston, per
15 Jerry Houston, and by
16 Lane, Powell, Moss & Miller, per
17 Wilbur J. Lawrence
18
19 Department of Labor and Industries, by
20 The Attorney General, per
21 Edward G. Gough, Robert G. Swenson, and Walter F. Robinson, Jr., Assistants
22
23 This is an appeal filed by the widow-petitioner on November 27, 1967, from an order of the
24
Department of Labor and Industries dated October 4, 1967, which rejected her claim for a widow's
25
26 pension. SUSTAINED.
27
DECISION
28
29 Pursuant to RCW 51.52.104 and RCW 51.52.106, this matter is before the Board for review
30
and decision on timely Statements of Exceptions filed by the widow-petitioner, the employer, and
31
32 the Department of Labor and Industries to a Proposed Decision and Order issued by a hearing
33
examiner for this Board on September 14, 1970, in which the order of the Department dated
34
35 October 4, 1967 was sustained.
36
The Board has reviewed the evidentiary rulings of the hearing examiner and finds that no
37
38 prejudicial error was committed and said rulings are hereby affirmed.
39
The issue presented by this appeal is whether the death of Alfred Morrill on May 29, 1967,
40
41 was the result of an industrial injury, namely, a bee sting suffered on May 26, 1967, during the
42
course of employment.
43
44 Our hearing examiner's order adequately set forth the medical aspects of the case, but did
45
not discuss the course of employment aspects.
46
47
1
12/7/70

1
The employer and Department contend on this appeal and in the exceptions that the
2
workman was stung by the bee during an independent act of his own which had no relation to the
3
4
employer's business or interest. We will set forth hereinafter the basis of the employer's and
5
Department's contention as concisely set forth in their exceptions to the Proposed Decision and
6
7
Order. We find merit in their contention.
8
The facts surrounding the bee sting are simple and essentially un-contradicted. Mr. Morrill,
9
10
the deceased workman, and two fellow workers, a Mr. Rye and Mr. Nelson Waddle, were working
11
as a team in falling and bucking on May 26, 1967. Mr. Rye had discovered honey in a "bee" tree.
12
13
After the three had eaten their lunch, Mr. Morrill was stung. (BR 65, 351, 352, 365) It is apparent
14
from the evidence that it was necessary for these workmen to reach into the tree to get the honey.
15
16
(BR 65, 368, 369) The taking of the honey was the independent idea of these three men. (BR 369)
17
Thus, Morrill was not stung while working or while eating lunch or while resting. The sting resulted
18
19
from Morrill's independently seeking honey for himself.
20
Under RCW 51.32.010, the widow's right to recover depends upon whether her deceased
21
22
husband was injured while he was acting within the "course of his employment." So far as here
23
material, "course of employment" is referred to in three sections of the Industrial Insurance Act.
24
25
RCW 51.08.013 defines the term as
26
". . . acting at his employer's direction or in the furtherance of his
27
employer's business . . . ."
28
29
RCW 51.32.015 provides that the benefits of the Act
30
31 ". . . shall be provided to each workman receiving an injury . . . during
32 the course of his employment and also during his lunch period as
33 established by the employer while on the jobsite. . . ."
34
35 RCW 51.36.040 contains similar language.
36
RCW 51.32.015 and RCW 51.36.040 were enacted in 1961 as sections 1 and 2 of Chapter
37
38 107, Laws of 1961. Prior to their enactment, the Supreme Court had held, as a matter of law, that
39
injuries occurring during the employee's lunch period were not compensable in cases where the
40
41 employee was not paid during the lunch period and was not subject to his employer's direction and
42
control. D'Amico v. Conjuista, 24 Wn. 2d 674 (1946); Mutti v. Boeing Aircraft Co., 25 Wn. 2d 871
43
44 (1946); Tipsword v. Department of Labor and Industries, 52 Wn. 2d 79 (1958). In Tipsword, the
45
court commented that its construction of the Act was harsh, and that Judge Jeffers' dissent in
46
47
2

1
D'Amico v. Conquista was more in keeping with the Act's purposes. In Tipsword, supra, Judge
2
Rosellini said, at pages 81-82:
3
4
"It seems to us that the construction which this court, in D'Amico v.
5
Conquista, supra, placed upon RCW 51.08.180 (designating that, in
6
order to be eligible for the benefits of this act, a workman must be in the
7
course of his employment), was much too narrow, and that an
8
interpretation of the statute which extends its benefits to a workman, the
9
nature of whose employment requires him to eat his lunch in the vicinity
10
of his job and incur the hazards which exist there, would be more in
11
accord with the spirit of the act. Judge Jeffers, dissenting in D'Amico v.
12
Conquista, supra, ably set forth the arguments in favor of such an
13
interpretation . . . ."
14
15
This was in effect an invitation by the Court for the Legislature to enact Judge Jeffers' dissent into
16
law. This is exactly what the Legislature did in enacting RCW 51.32.015 and RCW 51.36.040 in
17
18
1961.
19
But Judge Jeffers pointed out in his dissent, not every injury occurring during the lunch
20
21
period is compensable even in those jurisdictions where coverage is extended to lunch periods. As
22
in cases of injuries occurring during regular work periods, an employee may remove himself from
23
24
the Act's protection during the noon hour if the injury results from the wholly independent act of the
25
employee for his own benefit or gain particularly where the employee's act has no connection with
26
27
the employee's work or meal and places him in a more dangerous position than was required of
28
him during the meal period. If this were not the case, the employee's coverage during the lunch
29
30
period would be greater than during his normal work periods. We believe the Legislature by
31
enacting RCW 51.32.015 intended to give the same coverage during the lunch hour as that
32
33
applicable during the work period.
34
In his dissent in D'Amico, Judge Jeffers quotes from Young v. Department of Labor and
35
36
Industries, 200 Wash. 138 (1939). Thus, Judge Jeffers says (24 Wn. 2d at p. 689):
37
"The opinion in the Young case continues:
38
39
"'Consulting the cases from other jurisdictions, we find many instances
40
in which employees have been injured during meal hours when they
41
were not actually at work. The general rule in such cases is that the
42
injury is compensable if the employee was, at the time, doing something
43
incidental to the duties for which he was engaged, but is not
44
compensable if the injury resulted from an independent act of the
45
employee having no connection with his work or his meal.' (Italics mine.)
46
47
3

1
"The opinion then quotes the following statement from 71 C.J. 739,
2
Section 456:
3
"'In accordance with the general rule that injuries to an employee while
4
he is doing something not strictly within his obligatory duty but which is
5
incidental thereto may be compensable, harm which befalls an
6
employee may be compensable when it occurs to him during the lunch
7
period or other meal period. However, harm sustained during a meal
8
period may not be compensable as arising out of and in the course of
9
employment when the harm results from an independent act of the
10
employee having no connection with his work or his meal, or from the
11
independent act of a third person, or when the harm is sustained by
12
reason of the employee's placing himself in a more dangerous position
13
than was required of him during the meal period, or where sufficient
14
evidence that harm sustained during the meal period was an accident
15
arising out of and in the course of the employment is lacking.' (Italics
16
mine.)
17
18 "The opinion continues:
19
"'The theory of the cases is that a period of rest, refreshment or other
20
temporary cessation from work, is not of itself sufficient to break the
21
continuity of employment, but that the independent act of the employee ,
22
which has no relation to the employer's interest, serves to break the so-
23
called nexus and to put the employee without the course of his
24
employment.'" (Court's emphasis.)
25
26
Thus, even where the benefits of the Act are not denied during lunch periods, a workman
27
28 removes himself from the Act's protection by voluntarily proceeding upon his own for his
29
independent benefit.
30
31 This is what the employer and the Department contend occurred here. Mr. Morrill was on his
32
own when he was stung. He went voluntarily to the "bee tree" to obtain honey for his own use and
33
34 benefit. The act of obtaining and removing honey from the "bee tree" had nothing to do with Mr.
35
Morrill's work for International Paper Company; the company received no benefit from the
36
37 employee's act. In every respect, removing the honey was the employee's own independent act
38
"having no connection with his work or meal." This independent act exposed Mr. Morrill to the
39
40 danger of bee stings, and if, in fact, he was allergic to bee stings, as the widow-petitioner contends,
41
he voluntarily placed himself "in a more dangerous position than was required of him during the
42
43 meal period." Clearly, under the rationale of Judge Jeffers' dissent, the bee sting was not an
44
"injury" in the "course of employment" covered by the Act.
45
46
47
4

1
The widow-petitioner's exceptions contend that her husband's death occurred when it did
2
because of the bee sting and therefore she is entitled to the benefits of the Washington Workmen's
3
4
Compensation Act, even though he had an arteriosclerotic heart condition. To prevail on this
5
theory, Mr. Morrill would have had to be stung in the course of his employment.
6
7
After consideration of the Proposed Decision and Order and the Statements of Exceptions
8
filed thereto, and a careful review of the entire record before us, we are persuaded that the
9
10
Proposed Decision and Order is supported by the preponderance of the medical evidence and is
11
correct in sustaining the Department's rejection of the claim.
12
13
The hearing examiner's proposed findings, conclusions and order are hereby adopted as this
14
Board's findings, conclusions and order and incorporated herein by this reference, and an
15
16
additional finding is made as follows:
17
5. Mr. Morrill removed honey from the bee tree on May 26, 1967 for his
18
own use, pleasure and benefit. He did not do so in furtherance of the
19
interests of the International Paper Company nor for its benefit. In
20
removing the honey, Mr. Morrill voluntarily and knowingly exposed
21
himself to bee stings, thus voluntarily placing himself in a dangerous
22
position having no relationship to his work or meal. At the time Mr.
23
Morrill was stung by the bee, he was outside the scope of his
24
employment.
25
26 It is so ORDERED.
27
Dated this 7th day of December, 1970.
28
BOARD OF INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE APPEALS
29
30
31

32
ROBERT C. WETHERHOLT Chairman
33

R. M. GILMORE Member
37
38 SPECIAL CONCURRING OPINION
39
I believe that the majority opinion is correct in finding that the hearing examiner's proposed
40
41 findings and conclusions should be adopted as I do not think the weight of the evidence supports
42
the widow-petitioner's theory that her husband's death was proximately caused by the bee sting
43
44 which he sustained during his lunch hour while an employee of this employer.
45
However, I will have no part in any effort to limit the coverage extended to injured workmen
46
47 under RCW 51.32.015. I cannot agree with what the majority has characterized as the legislative
5

1
intent in enacting RCW 51.32.015. I am unaware of any case law which supports this idea. I can
2
find only one exception to the complete coverage of injured workmen during their lunch period
3
4
(RCW 51.32.020), if such injury or death was the result of the workman's deliberate intention to
5
produce such injury or death, or while engaged in the commission of a crime. There is no showing
6
7
in this case that there is any applicability of this statute and I see no reasonable basis to impose
8
limitations upon the right of injured workmen to receive benefits during their lunch hour which are
9
10
not specifically established by statute. The argument that this deceased workman was outside the
11
scope of his employment when stung is not material. The statute expressly provides for coverage
12
13
under the Act to workmen who are injured during the course of their employment and also during
14
their lunch period. It would seem to me that it was contemplated by the Legislature that a workman
15
16
would not be in the course of his employment at such times, therefore the explicit coverage.
17
Therefore, I cannot join with the majority in the amendment to the proposed findings,
18
19
conclusions and order of the hearing examiner by the inclusion of an additional Finding No. 5.
20
21
Dated this 7th day of December, 1970.
